basic_info.name: The Call (Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst)
basic_info.location: Serpentine North Gallery, London, UK (4 October 2024 - 2 February 2025)

practice_description.medium: AI choral installation, sound, sculpture, interactive AI model
practice_description.practice_summary: Three interconnected installations (The Hearth, The Wheel, Oratory) that reframe AI as an extension of collective singing traditions, using custom choral AI models trained on consented recordings from 15 UK choirs performing Sacred Harp hymns.
practice_description.methodology: Herndon and Dryhurst composed a songbook of hymns and singing exercises, then conducted a choral dataset tour across the UK in Spring 2024 (Belfast, Leeds, Bristol, Beith, and other cities) recording 15 professional and community choirs via a multi-channel recording protocol. The AI models (Choral Diffusion) were developed in collaboration with IRCAM-STMS (Nils Demerle, Mateo Fayet, Robin Meier, Philippe Esling) with machine learning support from Stability AI (Zach Evans, CJ Carr). A pioneering Data Trust was established to give choir participants governance over how the resulting AI models are deployed. The project treats the entire pipeline -- from recording protocol to data governance to AI training to installation -- as a unified artwork.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: The Call is a paradigmatic example of art-as-substrate for a graph-curated generative exhibition: it produces living AI models whose outputs are shaped by relational structures between choirs, communities, and governance protocols. Its approach to data trust governance directly models how A(DAI) might handle consent and collective intelligence.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. The choral AI models produce continuous generative output that could function as substrate material. The Hearth transforms GPU cooling fans into a pipe organ playing AI-generated hymns -- computation's byproducts become the art's ground layer.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Yes. The work is fundamentally relational: 15 choirs contribute to a shared dataset, and the AI models produce outputs that are composites of collective vocal input. The call-and-response structure is inherently graph-like, with each choir as a node contributing to a shared model.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Yes. The interactive Oratory component allows visitors to contribute their voices in real-time, with the AI harmonizing and layering new inputs. The work continuously evolves through participation.

works.title: The Hearth
works.description: Acoustic organ built from GPU cooling fans arranged like a pipe organ, filling the gallery with AI-generated hymns. At the organ's centre is an engraving of an infant blowing a lur (ancient wind instrument). Transforms computational infrastructure's byproducts into musical installation.
works.relevance: Demonstrates how infrastructure itself (GPU fans, heat, noise) becomes artistic material -- directly relevant to A(DAI)'s interest in infrastructure as creative medium.

works.title: The Wheel
works.description: Spherical chandelier-like installation in the South Powder Room with gilded panels engraved with imagery from the recording tour, serving as symbolic centre for the choral data.
works.relevance: Physical manifestation of a data provenance record -- the journey of data collection made visible as sculptural object.

works.title: Oratory (Interactive Choral AI)
works.description: Interactive installation where visitors contribute their voices and the choral AI model harmonizes them in real-time, creating an experience akin to joining a choir.
works.relevance: Live demonstration of human-AI collective composition, where individual contributions are woven into a collective output -- core A(DAI) Sense Room principle.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: The Call treats protocols as artistic medium at multiple levels: the recording protocol (how choirs are captured), the Data Trust protocol (how participants govern their data), and the AI training protocol (how models are built from consented data). The entire governance and technical pipeline is the artwork.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: A Data Trust governance structure where choir participants collectively determine how their recordings and derived AI models are used, shared, and protected. Also developed Choral Diffusion -- custom choral AI models. The Data Trust was incubated by Serpentine's Future Art Ecosystems project with support from King's College London Centre for Data Futures and RadicalxChange.

commons_orientation.licence_model: commons-based (CC-BY-NC-SA recommended by research findings for the choral dataset)
commons_orientation.commons_summary: The project is fundamentally commons-oriented. It established a Data Trust where 15 choirs collectively govern their data rather than ceding it to corporate interests. Research from a NeurIPS 2024 paper on the project found 92% of participants preferred choir-level (group) credit over individual credit (34%), and recommended CC-BY-NC-SA licensing. The artists previously built Spawning (haveibeentrained.com, Kudurru, Source.Plus) -- consent infrastructure for AI training data.

governance_model.governance_detail: Data Trust model with an appointed data intermediary (Jennifer Ding) who helps choir members exercise agency over dataset and model deployment. The trust includes an elected data trustee who makes decisions on behalf of the group, analogous to an elected representative. Led by Victoria Ivanova, Jennifer Ding, Eva Jager, Ruth Waters, and Mercedes Bunz at Serpentine Arts Technologies.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Explicit, participatory consent. Choirs were recorded through a deliberate protocol tour with full knowledge of intended AI training use. The Data Trust gives participants ongoing governance over how recordings are used. This builds on the artists' prior work: Have I Been Trained (2022, opt-in/out tool for AI datasets), Kudurru (data-defence network blocking AI scrapers), and Spawning (consent layer for AI).
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Collective and distributed. Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst are the lead artists, but the work explicitly positions the 15 choirs as co-creators with governance rights. Scientific collaboration credited to IRCAM-STMS and Stability AI teams. The NeurIPS research showed participants valued group recognition over individual credit.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: The installation had fixed elements (Hearth, Wheel) that played continuously, alongside the interactive Oratory where visitor voice input triggered real-time AI harmonization. The underlying AI models persist beyond the exhibition and are governed by the Data Trust for future use.

data_materiality.data_sources: Multi-channel recordings of 15 UK choirs singing Sacred Harp hymns (19th-century American shape-note tradition derived from old English choral music). Herndon and Dryhurst composed a specific songbook of hymns and singing exercises for the recording protocol.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Fully consented. Custom dataset created specifically for the project through a deliberate recording tour. Governed by a Data Trust structure. No scraped data. The Sacred Harp tradition itself is public domain (19th century).

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: The Choral Diffusion models operate in learned latent spaces of choral vocal timbres. The AI models generate new choral arrangements by navigating these learned vocal spaces, producing outputs that are interpolations and transformations of the training data.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Primarily audio, but the installation combines sound with physical sculpture (Hearth, Wheel) and visitor interaction.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Three distinct gallery spaces at Serpentine North: The Hearth (main gallery -- GPU fan organ filling the space with AI hymns), The Wheel (South Powder Room -- chandelier sculpture), and Oratory (interactive voice contribution space). The installation transforms a classical gallery into an immersive sonic environment.

interoperability.composability: The choral AI models could theoretically be exposed as APIs or used as inputs for other generative systems, subject to Data Trust governance. The recording protocol and Data Trust framework are replicable methodologies. The Choral Diffusion model architecture is a research output.
interoperability.technical_openness: Hybrid. The Data Trust governs openness -- the choir participants collectively decide whether models and datasets are shared. Research findings suggest CC-BY-NC-SA licensing. The scientific collaboration with IRCAM suggests academic publication norms.

technical_approach.stack: Choral Diffusion (custom AI models developed with IRCAM-STMS), machine learning support from Stability AI, multi-channel recording protocol, GPU cooling fan acoustic organ, custom sculpture fabrication

network_position.scene_affiliation: Berlin experimental music/art scene, Serpentine institutional ecosystem, AI art, protocol art, commons/data governance, choral music communities across the UK
network_position.connections: Serpentine Arts Technologies (commissioner and collaborator), Fellowship.xyz (represents Herndon/Dryhurst), Starmirror (sister work at KW Berlin), Spawning/Have I Been Trained (prior consent infrastructure), IRCAM (scientific collaboration), Stability AI (ML support), Feral File (Herndon/Dryhurst exhibited there for MoMA Sound Machines)

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: The Call is a primary reference artwork for A(DAI)'s Sense Room concept. Its Data Trust governance model is directly applicable to how A(DAI) might handle contributor consent. The choral AI models demonstrate art-as-substrate and collective intelligence coordination. The project's methodology (recording protocol, data governance, AI training pipeline) is a template for how A(DAI) could commission participatory intelligence-generating artworks.
